readerTitle: The coffee club that couldn't get past 400
caseNote: 가상 사례 (원두 정기배송 로스터리, 사무실 커피 공급 B2B 서비스) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 구독 사업은 '얼마나 들어오나'보다 '얼마나 머무나'로 천장이 정해지고, 연간 할인은 물건이 매달 나가는 사업에서 더 비싸다.
misconception: 신규 가입이 꾸준하면 구독 사업은 계속 큰다. 연간 결제는 할인을 줘도 무조건 이득이다.

sources.text: 구독 사업의 표준 개념 (이탈률과 정상 상태 고객 수, 월간·연간 결제)

factChecks.note: 정상 상태 고객 수 = 월 신규 ÷ 월 이탈률. 40 ÷ 0.10 = 400명, 이탈률 5%면 40 ÷ 0.05 = 800명. 현재 400명 × 10% = 월 40명 이탈로 신규 40명과 같음.
평균 구독 기간 ≈ 1 ÷ 월 이탈률 = 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10개월(근사치). 월간 고객 기대 매출 $20 × 10 = $200, 봉투당 원가 $8(원두·포장·배송) × 10 = $80, 남는 돈 $120.

cards.title: The coffee club that couldn't get past 400
body: A small roaster ships a bag of fresh beans to subscribers every month for $20. Forty new people sign up every month, like clockwork.
A year later, the roaster still has about 400 subscribers. Nothing is broken. Nobody is complaining. So where did the growth go?

image.label: A coffee bag on a doorstep, with a counter stuck at 400
image.brief: 현관 앞에 놓인 원두 봉투 하나. 옆에 디지털 카운터가 "400"에서 멈춰 있고, 한쪽 문으로 사람들이 들어오고 다른 쪽 문으로 같은 수만큼 나가는 장면. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Why has the club stopped growing?
body: The roaster has 400 subscribers. It signs up 40 new ones each month. About 10% of subscribers cancel each month.

options.feedback: Possible someday, but signups haven't slowed. The numbers already explain the stall without it.
Right. This is **the math of retention**: 10% of 400 is 40 cancellations a month, exactly matching the 40 new signups.
Cutting price would shrink what each bag earns, and 40 people a month are happily paying it. The leak is on the way out, not the way in.

cards.title: Every subscription business has a ceiling.
body: Divide new signups by the monthly cancellation rate. That's where the customer count settles. The roaster isn't failing. It has simply arrived.
cards.callout: Halving cancellations doubles the ceiling without one extra ad.

cards.title: Ask why people leave.
body: The roaster calls ten people who cancelled. Most say the same thing: unopened bags were piling up in the cupboard. They liked the coffee. They just drank less than a bag a month.
So the fix isn't a louder ad. It's letting people choose every six weeks, or skip a month with one tap.
A skipped month earns nothing. But a customer who skips and stays keeps the ceiling high. A customer who cancels is gone.

cards.title: Should the roaster sell an annual plan?
body: Monthly is $20. Each bag costs $8 in beans, packaging and shipping. At 10% monthly cancellation, the average subscriber stays about 10 months and leaves $120 after costs.
The roaster is considering a prepaid year. What's the smartest version?

options.text: $200 a year (two months free), pushed as the main option
options.feedback: You get cash up front, but 12 bags cost $96, so you keep $104. That's less than the $120 from an average monthly customer, and your loyal $240 customers switch too.

options.text: $228 a year (one month free), next to monthly with easy skips
options.feedback: This is **annual vs monthly** with real costs counted. You keep $132 a year, gain committed customers, and don't give away much to people who'd stay anyway.

options.text: No annual plan; it only complicates things
options.feedback: Simple, and no discount leaks. But you give up upfront cash that could buy green beans in bulk, and a year of commitment.

cards.title: Annual discounts cost more when you ship something.
body: The customers most likely to pay for a year are the ones who would have stayed a year anyway. For them, the discount is pure giveaway: $40 each at $200.
And every extra month means another bag of real coffee leaving the building. Prepaid money also comes with a promise. If someone moves away in month three, you may owe a refund.
cards.softwareNote: In software, an extra month of service costs almost nothing to deliver, so annual discounts are cheaper to give. The loyal-customer giveaway still applies.

cards.title: Now it's an office coffee service.
body: You supply beans and machine upkeep to offices for $500 a month. You have 50 office clients. About 2% cancel each month, roughly one office. Your one salesperson signs 3 new offices a month.
Where should next quarter's effort go?

options.feedback: **The math of retention** says your ceiling is 3 ÷ 2% = 150 offices. You're at 50 and growing by 2 a month, so more signups raise the count fastest right now.

options.text: Launch a program to cut cancellations to 1%
options.feedback: It lifts the ceiling to 300, which matters later. But with churn already low and the ceiling far off, it adds less this quarter than new clients.

options.text: Move every client to an annual contract at 15% off
options.feedback: **Annual vs monthly** cuts both ways: clients who rarely leave would cost you $3,750 a month in discounts to prevent about one cancellation.

cards.softwareNote: Software companies run the same check: divide monthly new signups by monthly churn to see whether growth or retention is the bottleneck.

cards.title: Know your ceiling before you choose your fix.
body: You used two ideas. **The math of retention:** signups ÷ cancellation rate shows where you'll stall, and whether to fix the way in or the way out. **Annual vs monthly:** a prepaid plan is only a win once you count what each extra month costs to deliver.
**Try it today:** take last month's new customers and divide by the share who left. Is your ceiling near or far?
